 Social Security COLA: The Impact on the Trust Fund and Retirement Benefits
 TheStreet Tue, November 17, 2026 at 2:41 PM MST Eric Boehm joins us to discuss Social Security COLA and its impact on the Trust Fund and retirement benefits. The conversation examines how annual benefit adjustments affect retirees, program costs, and the long-term outlook for Social Security. 
 Video Transcript 00:01 Speaker A Eric, it's so great to see you. Thanks for popping by the program this morning. 
 00:05 Speaker B Jeff, thanks for having me on. Really glad to be here. 
 00:07 Speaker A Well, the pleasure's all mine and I have to point out I like the books behind you of Robert Heinlein. I'm a big fan of of that and I know you told me that there's a lot of Easter eggs there uh behind you. So, um very kudos to you and the Reason Foundation for putting that together. 
 00:30 Speaker B Yeah, there's there's a lot of good books back on that shelf. A lot of good recommendations there. 
 00:34 Speaker A Yeah, there we go. Well maybe you should do your own book maybe Reason should do its own book show. Maybe you do. That's not a bad idea. Maybe we should, yeah. There you go. Cody, are you listening? All right, anyway, um, let's talk about so yesterday we as I was telling you, we had the Tax Foundation on talking about the new tax brackets. Social security obviously came up because there's a tax that's part of that that and social security is becoming insolvent. 
 01:03 Speaker A Um let's talk about this Cola, this cost of living adjustment. You had some interesting thoughts in your piece. 3.6% for this year, announced for this year by social security. I want to get your top line reaction to that though. What go give us your top line reaction. 
 01:21 Speaker B Yeah, I mean I think well so so first just to lay out the numbers for people who maybe don't pay a lot of attention to this. retirees are getting that 3.6% cost of living adjustment that you mentioned. That's uh it's 0.8 percentage points higher than it was last year and it's nearly a full percentage point, 0.9 percentage points higher than what social security thought they were going to pay. Now that Cola is driven by, uh it's mostly driven by inflation. The way social security calculates that adjustment is not exactly the same as inflation, but the two things are pretty closely linked. 
 01:54 Speaker B And I think one thing that that this is like I I try to raise this issue every year when this Cola gets announced because there's this idea out there that retirees are living on fixed incomes or that social security benefits are somehow fixed and that, you know, as as uh, you know, prices rise, retirees are squeezed. And it's actually quite the opposite. Uh retirees, people who who benefit from social security are getting uh this, you know, cost of living adjustment. They get one every single year. 
 02:27 Speaker B Um and so that actually, you know, is is in some ways quite a lot bigger than what some workers might be expecting to get this year, particularly when you're an environment like we are right now where inflation has been running hotter than uh average wage increases, which has been true for the past uh several months, much of the past year. Uh and so I think that just sort of punctures one of these like common myths out there about social security that like the benefits are somehow eroding away or they're somehow not generous enough when uh it's actually quite the opposite. 
 02:59 Speaker A So, let me ask you about the what is the impact? So, when you are paying 3.6% more in in terms of this cost of living adjustment, what is the impact to the trust fund? So I'm thinking about everyone has been talking about this 2032 number, if you read it in in USA today or you read it at reason, everyone's talking about it, the trust is going to go, I guess to a point where they're going to have to do haircuts. What is what is this number do to that? 
 03:38 Speaker B Yeah, that's right. I mean, obviously this increases the money that social security pays out in benefits, right? So social security is just a straight transfer program. It collects money from the paychecks of workers and it transfers that money out to retirees. But the problem is for many years now, social security has been running a deficit. It's been paying out more than it takes in. Uh this year for example, it's going to uh it collected about $1.4 trillion in payroll taxes. It's going to spend uh nearly $1.7 trillion. 
 04:13 Speaker B So there's a gap there obviously, and that gap has been eating away at the so-called trust fund, which is sort of the extra savings. It's it's really just an accounting gimmick actually, but the extra savings that Social security has. Now when that trust fund runs out, when that accounting gimmick no longer works in 2032, uh that's the current projection, then the program will only be able to pay out as much money as it takes in. So instead of, you know, for example this year, 1.4 came in, uh 1.7 went out, right? 
 04:47 Speaker B In 2032 that'll no longer be possible. Only the amount that comes in annually will be able to be transferred out and that means you're going to have the what it effectively means is that you're going to have a a pretty significant cut on the benefit side starting that year. Current estimates from the trustees that run social security is that the uh benefit cut will be about 20 to 23%. That obviously will differ depending on what your specific benefits are, but on average that means about a 6,000 annual cut to beneficiaries. 
 05:22 Speaker B And this is what will happen if nothing changes. Again, this is one of these myths I think we hear about social security over and over again. You hear politicians say, oh, you know, we don't need to we don't need to touch social security, we don't need to reform social security. We just need to let the program work. If you do that, if you do nothing, this is the path that we are on. There will be automatic benefit cuts across the board that will hit every single beneficiary. 
 05:51 Speaker A So knowing that and and there was a vote, I can't remember the name of the bill but I think it was earlier this year, the year prior expanding the benefits to government workers. So that I would assume adds to that the the the the cost that the costs that we're talking about it. So with this 3.6%, I I would imagine that this is set by the social security administration. Does the Congress again, I need, you know, it's been a while since I've been in schoolhouse rock for those who are old enough to remember. 
 06:29 Speaker A But who sets the street this cola? Is it the Social Security administration? Is it Congress? Is it a combination thereof? 
 06:38 Speaker B Yeah, so it's it's like I said at the beginning, it's sort of uh it's a it's similar to inflation, but it's not the same. They don't use the same measure of inflation. They're actually a lot of different ways to measure inflation. When we sort of colloquilly talk about inflation, we talk about the consumer price index is typically the measure we're using. The social security administration uses the uh consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers. This is like a subset of the consumer price index. Um yeah, it's relatively narrow. 
 07:07 Speaker B And uh and it's it's actually a bit it's a bit more generous by using that rather than just using uh rather than using the more general uh consumer price index or as some people would prefer to see it, a change made so that we go into using uh chained CPI, which is a again a different way to measure inflation, but a more accurate one that covers something like 93% of all workers as opposed to the more narrow uh measurement that's used by the program now. 
 07:39 Speaker B So, uh yeah, that's certainly a change that should happen. Uh regardless that's that's a change that doesn't necessarily affect the underlying math. It doesn't affect the underlying problems with social security, which all ultimately go back to the fact that it's a transfer program, taking money from the paychecks of workers and sending money to the to retirees and that ultimately the math just isn't math on that. Uh but making those sort of changes about how these cola are calculated or as as I wrote in that piece and what I would prefer to see is just eliminate the colas all together and and fundamentally change the way the program works. 
 08:14 Speaker B But if you're going to change the the calculation there, that would help uh it would help extend the solvency of the program. It would also just be a more accurate way of making sure people are uh being protected against inflation, uh but without, you know, putting too much of an additional burden on the workers who are paying for the program. 
 08:34 Speaker A So to make that change that we're talking about, changing the CPI calculation, is that take an act of Congress to do that and and or is that something that the minister I would imagine it would, right? Wouldn't you need 
 08:50 Speaker B Yeah that's something that Congress would have to do, right? That would be presumably a piece of whatever big social security package ends up getting done in the next uh six or seven years to address this coming shortfall that we've been talking about in in 2032. Uh Congress is going to have to do something because I don't think, well, I mean, I guess they could do nothing and just let the program hit the wall, but I I don't think that's realistic. really a realistic solution. So this is this is one idea among many that could be included in a in a kind of overall reform package. 
 09:27 Speaker A So, so, do you think uh and and again, I don't want to put you in a corner. I'm not asking you to maybe prognosticate here, but do you think that we've got a new Congress, January. Well, number one, do you think it take gets this gets taken up in the old Congress or this current Congress or the lame duck session, or do you think this is something that comes up in 2027, knowing that 2032 is only really less than six years away. 
 09:59 Speaker B Yeah, I'm actually somewhat surprised that there hasn't been more talk about this when you think about the timeline here. 2032 still sounds like the future to me, right? It sounds like it's far away. Right, the senators that were elected in November, the senators that were elected in that election we just had two weeks ago, their term will be still ongoing. It's a six-year term when we hit 2032. So we are now at the point in time where the the politicians that we are voting for uh in this cycle, certainly in the 2028 presidential cycle 
 10:37 Speaker B Uh these are going to be the people that will have to solve that problem and yet there really just isn't a lot of talk about this. So I'm kind of surprised by that. I I am, you know, would be shocked if you see anything in the lame duck session of Congress dealing with this this year. Quite frankly, I'd be kind of shocked if you see anything even in the next couple of years uh in Congress. Although, you know, maybe there's there's the hope that a a Democratic Congress and Republican administration could get together and kind of find, you know, some some middle ground on this because that's ultimately politically what you're going to need, I think to solve this problem. 
 11:13 Speaker B is it's going to need to be uh both both parties, you know, agree to to do something that probably annoys a significant subset of their voters on both sides, but that allows for some sort of compromise to happen. Uh when you have unified government, there's uh, you know, with either party in full control. I think there's just not a lot of incentive to fix the problem because both sides, this has been the case for many years now, both sides have just kind of been hoping to blame the other side for uh the mess that is that is coming. 
 11:51 Speaker A Yeah, I mean they just want to, you know, it's about retaining control, growing power. I mean, I I think a lot of us get that. if not, then we're find we're finding that out. Um, you know, I I I guess where where I kind of come with this and and, you know, is that is it really up to the retirees today and in the future, everyone, all of us are paying into it or or will pay into it. If you're a worker coming out of college today, you're going to be you're paying into it and and you're getting your first job. So you have a vested interest. 
 12:35 Speaker A Um isn't this something that we wouldn't we all collectively uh whether we're getting benefits today or in the future, want to kind of come to kind of some kind of compromise knowing that the way the demographics are in the country and will be, we're upside down. It it can't work. 
 13:00 Speaker B Yeah, that's right. I mean, social security was never designed for the, you know, the country the way it is today with the, you know, the numbers the way they exist. We have way fewer workers per retiree now than we did when the program was invented certainly and and way fewer even than when the program was last significantly overhaul in the early 1980s. Um and I I think the story here, kind of the under appreciated story here is the fact that we've known that this uh this fiscal cliff for social security was coming in the 2030s. 
 13:35 Speaker B We've known this since the 1980s. Honestly, there has been you know, Reason magazine has written about this. other publications have written about this now for decades saying, uh, you know, something is going to need to be done in the early to mid 2030s to uh either reform or end or extend social security. We're going to need to come together to have some sort of political compromise. Um and there's been like 40 years of politicians have kicked the can down the road on this and uh the fact that nothing has gotten done now really limits the options quite frankly when it comes to what can be done because the more time you have to phase in various changes 
 14:14 Speaker B obviously makes it a little bit easier to accomplish those things. So, uh you've had yeah, you've I mean you've literally had an entire generation of politicians come through Washington, an entire generation of uh of who are now really the retirees in the country, the people who are going to be the ones who see their benefits cut, uh who have failed to uh fix this problem. And so I think that's that's got to be part of the equation when we talk about this. Uh it's it's the easy solution in many ways will be to just say, oh, we're going to raise taxes on workers to fund the program to to fix the shortfall. 
 14:49 Speaker B Um and I think that's absolutely the wrong way to go. I think benefit cuts or changes to the benefit structure have to be a significant part of what uh the any sort of reform package looks like for social security, um because it's the retirees who had a chance for 40 years to fix this problem and failed to do it. 
 15:10 Speaker A Let me ask you and this is not covered in your piece. so forgive me if you don't want to address this, but is there, you know, when social security was founded in the 19 20s, late 1920s after the Great Depression and the reform acts of of the Roosevelt administration, the 401K system, the private retirement system really didn't exist except for maybe defined benefit plans. That defined benefit structure has kind of gone away for other for many reasons, we don't have to talk about that here. 
 15:43 Speaker A Is there a role for the private retirement system? I'm thinking 401K, 403B, government 457 to maybe supplement because even if you don't have access to a 401K, sorry, it's a long winded question, but if you don't have access to a 401K, you can contribute to an IRA. There are many state run Auto IRA programs today. It's something. So, the question is, can that support make up the difference here? Sorry, go ahead. 
 16:17 Speaker B Yeah, no, I think that's I think that's exactly right. I think private private retirement savings uh obviously make up a huge chunk of the difference here and and doing a, you know, we've done a I think phenomenal job as a country to get people into private retirement savings accounts. That's the that's certainly the way to go. Um and that for any younger worker, you know, who's looking at the finances of social security, anybody. I'm not that young anymore. I'm going to be 40 next year, but when I came out of college, you know, I didn't think I was going to get social security and I still don't think I'm going to get social security. 
 16:49 Speaker B So, uh that's been a priority for me ever since I started working is to, you know, put away what I can. I think that's obviously very important. And I think it also just changes, you know, there's there's a shift that happens, I think mentally when you have private retirement savings being the priority, right? I think one of the reasons why people get so worked up and so angry and so uh you know, intense about social security is that is that they don't have any control over it, right? I think everybody knows that oh, this could be taken away, this could go away. 
 17:28 Speaker B It's it's up to politicians and and officials in Washington and and various other people to decide how much I get when I retire. I don't I I I don't have any control over that ultimately. I've been having this money taken out of my paycheck for decades and yet I have no actual understanding of of where that money is and how much of it I can get back. Um and so that creates fear in people and uncertainty in people and that I think drives a lot of the political conversations around social security. 
 18:04 Speaker B You know, with my private retirement savings, my IRA and my 401K and those programs, I can log in uh today, I could log in right now while we're having this conversation, right? And see the amount of money that's in that account and that belongs to me. I have a property right to that money, which simply isn't true with social security. And so yeah, I mean steering people towards uh more private retirement savings and and just sort of encouraging people to take care of themselves uh when it comes to planning for the rest of your life. That's that's the way out of this. 
 18:41 Speaker B And it's not just, you know, it's not just a financial solution, it's also in some ways a political solution because it allows you to feel more secure in what you have and you know, not to have to rely on the politicians to make the right decisions. 
 18:55 Speaker A Yeah, well, I I completely my personal opinion is, I completely agree. Eric, we're going to have to leave it there. Hey, great article, great piece. Thanks for joining us and we look forward to having you back on the program again very soon. 
 19:10 Speaker B Thanks so much, Jeff. I'd love to do it again. Thanks. 
 19:12 Speaker C Well, thanks for watching and don't forget, we're back again tomorrow morning with another great expert and another great topic. You can tune in right here Monday through Sunday at 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time.
